title: Parachute & Ball Games
strapline: One billowing canopy, a basket of balls and everyone needed — games that only work when we play them together.
intent: Develop throwing, catching, rolling and kicking — sending and receiving with growing accuracy.
Build shared attention and listening: parachute games collapse (literally) unless everyone tunes in together.
Learn the shape of a game with rules — waiting for your colour, your name, your turn to run under.
Strengthen shoulders, grip and whole-body timing through lifting, rippling and holding the canopy.
Experience being one essential part of something the whole group makes together.
Bring number into movement — counting shakes, bounces, and balls popped off the canopy.
implementation: Start every parachute session with the same gathering song so children know the game-space has opened.
Give instructions in two clear parts and wait — 'hold your edge tight, and when I say three, lift' — then relish the whoosh together.
Call quieter children's names for the run-under moments so the game hands them a brave, celebrated turn.
Match the ball to the learner: big soft balls for new catchers, smaller ones as hands get quicker; roll before bounce before throw.
Narrate technique lightly: 'You watched the ball all the way into your hands.'
Let older children call the game — handing over 'popcorn!' or 'mushroom!' makes them the rule-keepers.
Close with a slow, silent floating-down finish so the group learns calm together as well as excitement.
key_questions: What happens to the balls if some of us shake gently and some of us shake hard?
How did you know it was your turn to run under?
What do your hands need to do to be ready for a catch?
How many shakes do you think it will take to pop every ball off — shall we count?
What game shall we play next — and how will everyone know the rules?
Why does the parachute need all of us holding on?

impact.text: Younger children kick, roll and fling balls with intent, chasing down the rebound and trying again.
Children catch a large ball more often than not, and run, dodge and stop within the crowded game space without collisions.
Children hold their edge, listen out for the call, and act on two-part game instructions — 'hold tight, then lift on three.'
Children join in the parachute songs with words and actions, and ask for favourites — 'can we do the mushroom one?'
Children wait for their colour, take turns fairly, and hold each other to the rules of the game — 'you have to wait for your name!'
The game keeps going because children negotiate — agreeing who's calling, whose turn is next, what happens when the ball goes over the fence.
Children count things that matter in the game — balls back into the basket one by one, shakes until the last ball pops off — and know the last number tells them how many.
Throwing and catching grow into genuine confidence and control, part of a body that loves to move.

enhancements: Popcorn game with a count — predict how many shakes to empty the canopy, then test it.
A washing-line target run: throw beanbags through hoops hung at different heights.
Cat-and-mouse under the parachute — one child underneath, one prowling on top of the ripples.
Colour-call swaps: 'everyone holding red, run under!' — listening with your feet ready.
Skittles made from filled water bottles for rolling practice with a satisfying crash.
A giant lycra sheet as a slower, stretchier alternative for bouncing one precious teddy.
Ball-and-spoon relay for older children — a slow game where control beats speed.

playing_exploring: Children throw themselves into whole-group games, feeling the pull of the canopy and the bounce of every ball.
They test what the parachute can do — trapping air, hiding underneath, rippling fast and slow.
active_learning: New catchers keep their eyes on the ball through miss after miss until the first clean catch lands.
Children hold their edge and wait through other children's turns because the game is worth it.
creating_thinking: Children invent variations — new colour calls, sillier songs, a two-teddy bounce — and teach them to the group.
They make predictions and check them: which shake pops the balls highest, how many skittles will fall.
